item.content:encoded:
The Phillies were bounced from the playoffs with a Game 3 Wild Card Series loss to the Braves on Thursday night. Given that the Phillies made the World Series in 2022 and have regressed in playoff performance since (NLCS in 2023, NLDS in 2024, NLDS in 2025 and WCS in 2026) along with a relatively old roster, there has been a stream of "end of an era" discussion on Friday.
It's not unreasonable. There are certainly . There are bound to be overreactions. I overreact a decent amount of the time, so I get it. It happens. We're often prisoners of the moment and emotion is a real thing.
I do want to push back on a specific idea, though, as floated by Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic:
Trading Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber? Don't love the idea, but everything needs to be under consideration. Everything.
Now, be sure that this isn't to attack the writer there, as I have the utmost respect for him and he even said he doesn't love the idea. I can see a lot of people running with this, though, and I'll offer up my opinion that this just isn't a feasible idea for the Phillies.
First off, Harper has a no-trade clause and it's been pretty clear over the last several years that he's now Philly through-and-through and doesn't want to go anywhere. Schwarber also has a no-trade clause with his 10-and-5 rights and now has a family with two young children.
Let's say either or both would accept a trade. Would it help the Phillies other than salary relief?
Schwarber is a 34-year-old designated hitter heading into 2027 with four years and $132 million left on his deal. How many teams would give the Phillies anything of value while also taking on a large portion of the salary? The answer is not that many and it might be zero.
Harper needs to permanently go back to first base and he'll also be 34 years old next season. He has five years and roughly $125 million left on his deal. Again, how many teams would give good value back to the Phillies and salary relief? The number is higher than with Schwarber, but not by much.
This isn't to say neither player is good. Both are very productive offensively. In fact, they were the Phillies' only two good hitters this season. Harper had a 131 OPS+ and Schwarber was at 128 with 100 being the average player at getting on base and hitting for power. No other qualified players on the Phillies were in the vicinity of Harper or Schwarber. Only Bryson Stott at 98 even approached league average. Brandon Marsh finished at 90, Alec Bohm 87 and Trea Turner 81. Yuck.
Schwarber and Harper are much more valuable to the Phillies than they would be to any other team, given the circumstances. And, unless the Phillies are going full-on rebuild, they might as well play out the contracts and try to win with them.
If you look at how things are set up for next season with the pitching staff, a rebuild doesn't make sense.
- Jesús Luzardo made a turn toward ace this season. He's under team control through at least 2031.
- Cristopher Sánchez will likely finish in the top three of Cy Young voting. He's under team control through at least 2032.
- Zack Wheeler showed flashes of being really good while returning from an incredibly tough surgical procedure. He's signed for one more season. He could well return to ace form.
- Aaron Nola doesn't have a tradeable deal, but hey, he had a 10-start stretch with a 2.10 ERA late in the season.
- There were still inconsistencies, but Andrew Painter, at age 23, made big strides during the season and perhaps turned a corner with in Game 2 vs. the Braves. Next year could well be a breakout.
That's a five-man rotation and maybe one of the very best in the majors.
Jhoan Duran is a top-three closer, too.
The starting point here is a great rotation and closer combination, along with Harper and Schwarber being excellent hitters. That's a better nucleus than most teams have. Ownership is committed to doing what it takes to land a winner for the city of Philadelphia and Dave Dombrowski is a front office executive who has proven he's good at making good teams into champions.
Keep taking as many shots at the postseason as possible in hopes that one of these years, the hot streak lines up properly for a championship. We've seen a well-timed hot streak pay off in recent years for teams like the Nationals, Braves and Rangers -- and maybe it'll be the Padres this year? -- so we know it can happen. Hell, the 2022 Phillies were right there.
The team defense needs to improve and there should be some tinkering with the position players, but the foundation here is far too strong to bail on Schwarber and/or Harper, especially when it wouldn't improve the big-league roster in the near-term.

The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles.
Now the defending back-to-back World Series champions are preparing for the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves beginning Saturday at Dodger Stadium. Atlanta advanced by defeating the Philadelphia Phillies in the Wild Card Series, setting up the Dodgers’ first postseason matchup with the Braves since the 2021 NL Championship Series.
Your 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers. pic.twitter.com/XYs9LzjRIb
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers’ five-day bye gave Dave Roberts and his staff time to prepare their roster, and while most of the pieces are already in place, there are still some important decisions to make before the 26-man NLDS roster is finalized. MLB reports that the final bench spot remains particularly unsettled, while the bullpen could also have an opening depending on the health of Edgardo Henriquez.
Who will make the Dodgers’ pitching staff?
The Dodgers’ biggest strength heading into October is their starting rotation. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, and Tyler Glasnow form a formidable group, although Roberts had not formally announced the order entering Friday.
Yamamoto is the leading candidate to start Game 1 against Atlanta. His normal rest schedule is one of the reasons the Japanese right-hander makes the most sense for the opener, as starting Saturday would also give him the chance to be available for a potential Game 5 on his usual rest.
#ITFDB presented by Toyo Tires. pic.twitter.com/TcKpliJrnR
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers also have several pitchers who could be used in relief despite spending much of the regular season as starters. Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Emmet Sheehan are among the options who could give Roberts additional flexibility out of the bullpen.
Edgardo Henriquez is another name to watch. The right-hander emerged as an important leverage option during the regular season before lower back discomfort ended his year prematurely. The Dodgers planned to have him face hitters during the bye, with an activation for the NLDS possible if he comes through the workout without any problems.
What will the Dodgers’ offense look like?
Shohei Ohtani will once again be the centerpiece of the Dodgers’ offense, but the situation is different from what it appeared to be when the original story was written.
Ohtani returned from the injured list in late September and played in each of the Dodgers’ final five regular-season games. He went 5-for-21 with eight strikeouts and one walk during that stretch, but Roberts said the team had no health concerns with its superstar heading into the postseason.
It’s Shotime! On this day in 2024, Shohei Ohtani started the 50/50 club.
This MomenTito’s in Dodger history presented by Tito's Handmade Vodka. pic.twitter.com/cxOEcJyPNK
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 19, 2026
Ohtani is expected to remain the designated hitter, with Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freddie Freeman at first base and Max Muncy at third. The Dodgers’ outfield is also largely established, with Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages expected to occupy the three spots.
The lineup could continue to feature some adjustments depending on the opposing starter. Against right-handed pitching, Ohtani has been used at the top of the order, while Betts has taken the leadoff spot against left-handers. That platoon is expected to continue into October.
Who's your Player of the Game? Comment your answer below! pic.twitter.com/tt6sVtGvWT
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 26, 2026
Who gets the final roster spot?
The Dodgers have several candidates competing for what could be their final bench spot: Josue De Paula, Dalton Rushing, Alex Call, and Hyeseong Kim. MLB’s postseason preview identified the decision as one of the biggest remaining questions for the club.
De Paula is intriguing after his impressive first taste of the Majors. The Dodgers’ top prospect hit .323 with seven RBIs and seven runs scored in 11 games before being optioned to Triple-A when Ohtani returned from the injured list. His performance was strong enough to keep him in the postseason conversation.
But Kim offers something different. His defensive versatility, speed, and ability to contribute off the bench could make him valuable in a playoff series, particularly if Roberts wants another defensive option late in games.
MLB.com Dodgers beat reporter Sonja Chen noted that both De Paula and Kim could have a chance to make the NLDS roster if Los Angeles carries 14 position players and 12 pitchers. The final decision could ultimately come down to whether the Dodgers prefer another impact bat or additional speed and defense.
Rushing and Call remain possibilities as well, meaning the Dodgers have not simply decided between De Paula and Kim.
The other variable is the pitching staff. If Los Angeles carries only 12 pitchers rather than the maximum 13, it would open another position-player spot and potentially allow Roberts to keep more of those candidates.
Dodgers are chasing history
There is plenty more than a division title at stake for Los Angeles. The Dodgers are attempting to become the first team since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 to win three consecutive World Series titles. They have already won three of the past six championships and enter October as the defending champions for the second straight year.
Their first obstacle is now set: the Atlanta Braves. The two teams will meet Saturday in Game 1 of the NLDS at Dodger Stadium, with Yamamoto the likely starter for Los Angeles. Before the first pitch, however, Roberts and the Dodgers still have a handful of decisions to make about exactly which players will be part of their attempt at a historic three-peat.

item.content:encoded:
With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts.
The Brewers and Padres could not be more different in how their teams were built. The Rays and Yankees don't like each other. The Guardians and White Sox also don't like each other. As for Braves-Dodgers? Well, there's plenty of recent history there. But which teams have the look of title contenders as we move deeper into October? Let's rank all eight remaining teams in terms of championship equity.
8. Chicago White Sox
The White Sox made it hard on themselves down the stretch, but Chicago is riding high after a first-round sweep of the Astros, with blessings from the Pope. Coming into the postseason, the White Sox were broadly dinged for their youth and inexperience. As fate would have it, though, the South Siders were significantly more poised than a seasoned Astros team.
Chicago's lineup performed top to bottom. They worked deep into counts and made smart, situational swings. The rotation is still a mess, and the bullpen is not much better, but there's a lovable underdog quality to this White Sox team that is hard to ignore. By default, the White Sox rank last here, but an ALDS matchup with the Guardians is perfectly winnable. Do not discount the possibility of a South Siders pennant run.
7. Cleveland Guardians
Cleveland has been there and done that. This team is always the AL Central champ, it feels like, even when the odds are stacked against them. The Guardians hit much better down the stretch after a brutal start to the campaign, while their pitching is a potential superpower. Parker Messick and Gavin Williams can match just about any aces blow-for-blow, and this bullpen always tends to perform.
The question now becomes: Can Stephen Vogt's squad translate their signature Guards Ball style to October? The answer for years now has been "no." Cleveland lacks thump in the heart of the order, but tends to execute the small things — bunts, base-running, two-strike hitting — better than anyone. Chicago's pitching staff is vulnerable and the Guardians have the edge in experience, but so did Houston. And the Astros' bats were much better. The outcome of this series will not shock me in either direction, to be frank.
6. Atlanta Braves
The Braves lineup struggled down the stretch but appeared to wake up against the Phillies, especially in the clincher. Atlanta has no shortage of offensive talent and a deep bullpen, with plenty of postseason experience to draw on. So why ranked so low?
Well, the rotation is a mess. Chris Sale is an elite 1A, but Tyler Mahle is questionable against better offensive teams (see: Dodgers) and their third starter is Grant Holmes behind an opener. Atlanta has seven starters on the IL and could struggle to build a bridge to the stellar back end of their bullpen in non-Sale starts. That said, if the Braves' bats heat up, perhaps it does not matter. There is a clear break in quality between Cleveland at No. 7 and the rest of the field. The Braves are very, very capable of mounting a deep run. Atlanta notably went 5-1 against the Dodgers this season.
5. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays just kept winning all season long. There was no more consistent force in the American League. We can quibble with the back half of their lineup and question the depth of their rotation, but the Rays are an extremely disciplined club with star power (Junior Caminero) and fundamental skills (Chandler Simpson, Jonny DeLuca) in equal measure.
Tampa is going to defend at a high level and run the bases with intent. Their pitching staff does not look so fearsome on paper, but Drew Rasmussen is a bonafide ace and Freddy Peralta looked more like himself in September. Whether this team can match the raw explosiveness of the Yankees' lineup is the swing factor. On the flip side, New York has a propensity for unforced errors that Tampa can ruthlessly capitalize on.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees are still waiting on Aaron Judge. New York stuffed its Wild Card roster with platoon bats and situational hitters, but Aaron Boone probably needs more pitchers for a five-game Divisional Series. The lineup exploded against the Red Sox, but Tampa will almost certainly manage its pitching staff better than Chad Tracy and Boston did.
New York is the best team in the American League on paper, even with all their injuries, but the bullpen is perilously thin and it's hard to trust this lineup completely. Ben Rice has caught fire at an optimal moment, so there's that. And the Yankees boast, by far, the most star power of any team west of Los Angeles. Whether it can all come together against a healthy, well-rested Rays team remains to be seen.
3. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers, almost without fail, dominate the regular season despite ownership's pervasive cheapness. This team knows how to develop talent in-house and locate value on the margins. There is no better-run small-market clubhouse in MLB. And yet, Milwaukee has consistently fallen flat in the playoffs. Whether or not this year is any different comes down to a couple factors.
First, Jacob Misiorowski helps. Milwaukee has the best pitcher in baseball and he may damn near guarantee a Game 1 win in the NLDS. The Brewers' bullpen is rock solid, too, while the depth of their rotation is respectable. Milwaukee's pitching can win ballgames. More importantly, there's less elite competition than usual; even the Dodgers are scuttling at the plate, while the entire American League is poked full of holes. The path has never been clearer for the Brewers, who compensate for limited slug with impressive plate discipline and savvy situational hitting. If Milwaukee can maintain its extraordinarily high baseline, there's reason to believe this could be the year it all clicks.
2. San Diego Padres
There are few stars I trust more in a high-leverage spot than Fernando Tatis Jr. The man just makes good things happen, whether he's using his power or his speed. San Diego's entire lineup, really, has come on strong in the final month. After sputtering for much of the regular season, the likes of Jackson Merrill and Manny Machado have apparently remembered how talented they are. Gavin Sheets and Ty France are improbably major contributors. On the pitching front, Michael King and Nick Pivetta tore through a loaded Cubs lineup. The Padres' bullpen is the best in baseball, so no team can more easily build a bridge between their frontline starters and the ninth inning.
San Diego's rotation depth is suspect; once Walker Buehler and Robbie Ray are asked to carry several innings, it could get dicey. But in terms of momentum and top shelf star power, the Padres clear the majority of the competition around them. It can't hurt that San Diego plays the Dodgers as well as any team, either. That matchup could ultimately define the 2026 season, assuming the Padres can out-slug the No. 1 seed Brewers.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
This shouldn't come as a shock. The Dodgers aren't as untouchable as their reputation suggests, but there's still only one team with Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow lined up on the mound. Meanwhile, Shohei Ohtani has proven his capacity for clutch swings time after time since arriving in Hollywood two years ago. Los Angeles has the best pitchers and the best player in MLB, with a star-studded lineup to boot. Mookie Betts, Kyle Tucker and Freddie Freeman weren't at the peak of their powers this season, but that's still a group worth trusting when every at-bat is magnified.
Los Angeles has depth, too. Josue De Paula is one of the most exciting young bats in baseball and the Dodgers barely have room for him on the roster. Alex Call and Dalton Rushing are useful as situational hitters. The primary concern is L.A.'s bullpen, but Rōki Sasaki, Kris Bubic and Justin Wrobleski — their excess rotation arms — should help the Dodgers cover innings when needed. The Dodgers are banged-up and very much vulnerable, but this is still the team to beat, full stop.

MLB playoff predictions 2026: Expert picks for every ALDS, NLDS series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
October has officially arrived, just in time for the MLB postseason to ramp up.
With all four Wild Card series now over — three of which ended in two-game sweeps — just eight teams remain alive in the pursuit of a World Series title, with the Guardians, Rays, Dodgers and Brewers entering the picture after watching the first round from home.
Some of baseball's biggest stars, from Shohei Ohtani and Jacob Misiorowski to Junior Caminero and Cam Schlittler, will be on full display for the division series. On both sides of the bracket, the question will be whether the teams carrying their Wild Card momentum can now take down a well-rested heavyweight.
With a chance to reset between rounds, the best-of-five ALDS and NLDS matchups begin Saturday. Who will advance to the championship series?
With Wild Card matchups in the rearview mirror, The Sporting News predicts the 2026 MLB division series matchups.
MORE: Complete MLB playoff schedule for 2026 postseason
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 2 Cleveland Guardians
You can certainly debate whether the Guardians (85 regular-season wins) or White Sox (84 regular-season wins) really belong on the postseason stage this season, with neither AL Central squad owning a ton of big-name star power. Regardless, the fact is that Cleveland and Chicago both find themselves with an opportunity to make a serious postseason run in a weaker AL bracket — and the White Sox have already taken advantage.
Chicago enters the ALDS the momentum of its first postseason series win since the 2005 World Series, proving in the Wild Card round that it has the power and pitching depth to challenge opponents. Cleveland, though, has better top-end starting pitching in Parker Messick, Gavin Williams and Tanner Bibee.
These two teams are well familiar with each other; the White Sox won the season series, 7-6. Cleveland's offense isn't very threatening, ranking last among all postseason teams in team OPS (.696) — this matchup will likely come down to how early the White Sox's bats can get to Guardians starters.
Saturday will mark the first time in MLB history that the Chicago White Sox and Cleveland have met in the postseason.
The White Sox began playing baseball in 1894 as the Sioux City Cornhuskers.
The Guardians began playing baseball in 1896 as the Columbus Buckeyes/Senators.
The fact that this is a divisional matchup means it will likely be close, but Chicago's momentum is hard to ignore, and there was only a one-win discrepancy between the sides in the regular season. The White Sox are finally building something serious, seemingly with a new hero every night. The power in Will Venable's lineup is dangerous enough to reach the ALCS.
Prediction: White Sox in 4
No. 4 New York Yankees vs. No. 1 Tampa Bay Rays
It's been clear since the start of the postseason that whichever AL East team emerged from the lower half of the bracket would be favored to reach the World Series. This is the heavyweight matchup of the two ALDS series, featuring elite starting pitching on both sides and some of MLB's premiere sluggers.
Of course, the massive question lingering over this matchup is how much, if at all, Aaron Judge will play for the Yankees. Even as the lower seed, if he's near 100 percent, it's hard not to view New York as the favorite to reach the ALCS; a healthy Judge, alongside Cody Bellinger, Luis Garcia Jr. and Ben Rice, takes Aaron Boone's lineup to a new level, capable of matching the all-around offensive excellence of Tampa Bay's quartet: Caminero, Yandy Siaz, Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson.
The Rays won this season series 7-6, but it may be the most evenly matched division series. Both sides can roll out a trio talented starters — New York with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried and Gerrit Cole, and Tampa Bay with Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and Shane McClanahan — to pair with deep offenses.
Yankees can line up their pitching as follows against the Rays:
Game 1: Gerrit Cole
Game 2: Cam Schlittler
Game 3: Max Fried
Game 4: Gerrit Cole
Game 5: Cam Schlittler
For two reasons, the Yankees are the pick here. For one, between Schlittler and arguably the best bullpen in baseball, New York is loaded with leverage arms. And the Yankees are also riding high off a dominant Wild Card series, biding time for Judge and Giancarlo Stanton to heal. Assuming those two sluggers can at least be used in some key at-bats, the Yankees' lineup is capable of changing games in an instant.
Prediction: Yankees in 5
No. 3 Atlanta Braves vs. No. 2 Los Angeles Dodgers
The Dodgers' path to becoming the first National League team to win three-straight World Series will begin with a matchup against a 94-win Braves squad fresh off a Wild Card win over the Phillies.
Los Angeles' rest advantage could be significant. Even if he's not pitching, Ohtani has been dealing with lingering injury concerns over the last few months. A week off between his last regular season game should only benefit him, not to mention the Dodgers' ability to line up their loaded starting rotation however they choose. With the Braves using Chris Sale in two games against Philadelphia, he may not be available early in the NLDS.
The Dodgers and Braves have built quite the postseason history. 👀🔥
2013 NLDS — LAD def. ATL
2018 NLDS — LAD def. ATL
2020 NLCS — LAD def. ATL
2021 NLCS — ATL def. LAD
2026 NLDS — ??? 🤔 pic.twitter.com/mHhbDO9gDX
The top of Atlanta's lineup is potent enough to make this an interesting series, and the team did beat the Dodgers five times in the regular season, but Ronald Acuna Jr., Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies will have to meet the moment in the NLDS. Yoshinobu Yamamoto has pitched well against Atlanta in his career, as have Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow.
Even if the Braves' bats can keep things close, it's hard to imagine Atlanta's pitching staff beyond Sale being able to contain Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Kyle Tucker and Mookie Betts over a five-game series. The Braves are a good team, but the Dodgers are far too talented to fall this early in the bracket.
Prediction: Dodgers in 4
No. 4 San Diego Padres vs. No. 1 Milwaukee Brewers
This matchup pins baseball's best team all season, Milwaukee, against one of its hottest over the past month, San Diego. While the Brewers are the clear favorites here, between the best starting pitcher in the game this season and a deep lineup that plays to contact, the Padres do pose some interesting challenges, going 4-2 against Milwaukee in the regular season.
On one hand, San Diego has stars made for October. As shown in the Wild Card round, when the top of the Padres' lineup is on, they're a hard team to beat — Fernando Tatis Jr., Manny Machado, Xander Boegarts, Ty France and Jackson Merrill can look like one of the best 1-through-5 groups in baseball at times. Add in an elite starter (Michael King) and a strong bullpen led by Mason Miller, and there's a path for the Padres to pull off a stunner here.
Most data has shown that the more of a threat a team is to hit the ball out of the yard, the better they'll fare in the postseason. If this is finally going to be the year the Brewers reach a World Series — putting an end to their cycle of regular season success with playoff shortcomings — they'll need to slug more. This is an offense that's outstanding at making contact and getting on base, but has also continually come up short in October and finished second-to-last in team home runs (154) in the 2026 regular season.
Chances are, Milwaukee won't only be able to rely on its strong pitching staff to reach the World Series. The Brewers' bats will need some extra-base hits. But with the Padres' lackluster starting pitching depth, this is still a series the Brewers can claim even if they're not pristine.
San Diego may have some top-end talent and momentum, but the Padres can't match Milwaukee's all-around depth.
Prediction: Brewers in 4

Tonight, the Atlanta Braves hosted the Philadelphia Phillies in a one-off game.
It was a highly anticipated division showdown.
The Phillies chose to put Aaron Nola on the mound… and early in the game, he didn't exactly live up to his managers' expectations.
In the first inning, after four batters, the score was 3-0. Michael Harris II hit a three-run homer after his teammates drew two walks.
Nola ended up pitching for less than two innings, even though his last start (which also went poorly) was five days ago. #RegularSeasonBreak
Ray Kerr, meanwhile, was slated to be an opener for the Braves. But he pitched longer than Nola in his first postseason start, thanks in large part to his defense.
The spin throw from Mauricio Dubón
The pick from Matt Olson
What a beautiful play by the @Braves defense! pic.twitter.com/fpAJ8LPwWx
— MLB (@MLB) October 2, 2026
Kerr didn't allow any runs in 3.1 innings of work. He was excellent.
The Phillies, meanwhile, quickly turned to Zack Wheeler. It was the right move, and manager Don Mattingly will have decisions to make if they advance to the Division Series.
The problem for the Phillies? Early in the game, they didn't put themselves in a position to worry about the series against the Dodgers.
Ozzie Albies went 5-0 with a two-run homer.
The Phillies pulled within 5-1, but the Braves maintained their five-run lead as Matt Olson hit a solo home run.
Then, with the score 6-2 and the Phillies gaining momentum, the Braves brought in Chris Sale. This likely makes up for his bullpen session between starts, but will he be able to pitch on Saturday? Sunday?
Sale hadn't pitched in relief in the playoffs since the 2018 World Series.
So the Braves have eliminated the Phillies. They'll face the Dodgers in the Division Series.

Cubs Video
It's every human's greatest (if, at times, subconscious or unwanted) wish to be understood—to have others really see us as we see ourselves and grasp what we believe gives life its meaning. The great danger of being a parent lies in either being too successful at imprinting your understanding of the world on your child (thereby passing down to them your biases, your shortcomings and your ossifications of thought, and making a clone of yourself, which will become an ill-adjusted being in a world very different from your own), or in feeling an eternal frustration that grows from the inability to communicate to someone so close that essential self-understanding that must be communicated to bring happiness.
I have always feared the former, more than the latter. I don't want my kids to be too much like me; I try to teach them mostly by pointing out my own mistakes and demanding that they avoid repeating them. Sometimes, though, that internal truth breaks containment, even when we don't want it to. In ways big and small, conscious and utterly accidental, we bare our souls to one another and a certain transference happens, whether we like it or not. In early August 2018, a YouTube user uploaded this highlight video of Javier Báez's season to that point. I loved it. Absent-mindedly, because my 5-year-old liked baseball and wanted something to watch, I showed it to him, too.
It was one of those moments. My son has never been the same; that video rewired his personality. Since then, he's been not only a rabid baseball fan, but a tenacious player—and on and off the diamond, this is the energy he seems to bring to life. It's a relief, in one way, because that's not the energy I bring to life, so he's certainly carving his own identity, but I lose some sleep over the possibility that I've turned him into a demon as obsessed with excellence and domination and creativity as Báez was in his best season, with (surely) less talent to give it all the proper outlets.
When the Cubs traded Báez a few years later, I was sad, and my son was even sadder. Of course, the playstyle on that tape was never going to age especially well, and Báez's more-bad-than-good years since have eased the pain of knowing the Cubs dealt him away, but the joy and ferocity of his game (at its best) was still absent from Cubdom, and the loss was felt, however inevitable I might have known it to be.
Right away, though, my son latched onto Pete Crow-Armstrong. The same sizzling intensity bends the light all around Crow-Armstrong, making him shimmer and raising the temperature (for good and ill) every time he's on the field. I was a bit slower to take the same depth of enjoyment from his game, because some of the rough edges around the game felt less endearing in Crow-Armstrong's case than in Báez's. Once I saw him reinvent himself at the plate (for the first time, way back in mid-2024), however, I was on board. He was adaptable, after all. He was intelligent, after all. He might even be more talented than Báez, and capable of applying that talent a bit more judiciously to his game.
That, of course, is what we've seen over the last two years. It was fun when Crow-Armstrong took off like a shot in 2025 and surpassed 20 homers and 20 steals before the All-Star break, but you could sense the recoil coming, and sure enough, he had a miserable final two months at the plate. The real breakout—the moment he went from a lovable star with two-way value to a generational guy—finally came this spring, as he adjusted to the bat speed he'd added over the offseason and altered his approach. That's when Crow-Armstrong became a player as winning-focused, clutch, and electrifying as Báez had been, although in a different way.
The internet has changed (read: worsened) over the last eight years, and no good analog for that Báez highlight reel is easy to find for Crow-Armstrong. Because everyone is desperately trying to monetize YouTube traffic for themselves, and because viewing hours determine monetization rates and pull in the money, you can watch four-minute highlights from MLB's official channel that include just one at-bat and the ensuing home-run trot, or 25-minute compilations of plays made by simply stringing together the full versions of original 30-second clips, but you won't find sleek, well-produced highlight videos as readily. So be it. I want to offer just one brief set of clips that illustrate the point, as a way of celebrating and remembering the magical season that just came to an end.
There's a big, grandiose way to do this, and maybe we'll do it another time. Today, we're doing the cozy minimalist version. Yes, there were a couple of months early this year when Crow-Armstrong played arguably the best defense in center field that the game has ever seen. Yes, there was a month in which he had an OPS of 1.249. Yes, there was one week in which he almost single-handedly won the Cubs four games, and yes, there were individual games scattered throughout the calendar in which he took the spotlight in ways we've hardly seen before. But I just want to talk about one game, in which he started the day 0-for-3 and the Cubs were slouching toward a 2-0 loss.
The date was August 6, which was supposed to be an off day. Because rain had postponed the team's series finale against the Blue Jays in June, though, Toronto had come back to town on a mutual blank space in the teams' schedules. It could have been a really tough moment in the team's season, but instead, they were riding high. Crow-Armstrong had won them a game against the Yankees over the weekend, and he'd just won them one the previous night against the Dodgers, showing Shohei Ohtani who was boss in the last moment at which anyone wondered which of the two would be the MVP of the National League.
It was a day game after a night game, though, and Crow-Armstrong went 0-for-3 through the first seven innings, with a strikeout. David Peterson pitched well, but gave up one run in the first, and the Jays tacked on a second tally in the seventh. Their near-automatic closer Louis Varland came on to save the game in the bottom of the ninth, with the cushion of that late run making things much less stressful. Crow-Armstrong wasn't even the tying run, when he led off the inning. Varland went right after his superstar opponent, getting ahead 0-2. Then, Crow-Armstrong slammed into one.
This was not one of his most vicious swings. It doesn't look like a case of cutting down with two strikes, but it was that, a little bit. He made sure he would connect solidly, rather than swinging for the fences (as he did for much of the year). The ball half-split the gap, too, and he probably could have had second on the play. Not playing for stats, though, he held at first, knowing his run meant too little to risk an attempt to advance. That set up Alex Bregman's dramatic, game-tying two-run homer, which sent the game to extra innings.
The Cubs should probably have won in 10 innings, but it went to 11. They held Toronto scoreless in the top half of each frame, so when Crow-Armstrong stepped in to lead off the bottom of the 11th, Carson Kelly stood at second base, carrying the winning run. He had a tough assignment, taking on lefty Brendon Little, and Little tried to leverage his platoon advantage. He also tried not to give Crow-Armstrong any chance to win the game for the Cubs—so much so that he threw him neither a fastball nor a strike the entire at-bat.
Every past version of Crow-Armstrong gets himself out in that situation, probably via strikeout. This version, though, showed a well-considered blend of intelligence and aggressiveness. He wasn't going to passively accept a walk. He felt he had a chance to win the game for the team. Nor, however, would he unduly expand his zone and leave Kelly at second with one down. He took two balls and fouled off a few two-strike offerings. Finally, on a 2-2 curveball that didn't dip quite low enough, he hit it right back through the box for a single. It could, even, have been the game-winner.
As it happened, though, Kelly shouldn't even have tried to score. He didn't get a clean enough break from second, and Myles Straw (who has a strong arm and charged the ball perfectly) got off too good a throw. The slow-footed Cubs catcher should have held at third, where a whole lot of possible things might have brought him home to walk it off. Instead, he ran into a pivotal first out.
Crow-Armstrong hadn't been anticipating a celebration or thinking too conservatively, though. The throw came through to the plate and thwarted Kelly, but when it did so, Crow-Armstrong advanced to second. Thus, the winning run was right back in scoring position—and now, it was a guy who was utterly determined to score it.
Few runners try to steal third with a lefty in the batter's box. Pitchouts are vanishingly rare in the modern game, but catchers have a clear lane to make a short throw when a lefty is at bat. All year, the league only attempted 70 steals of third from the seventh inning on. At that moment, in early August, the Cubs had only attempted one such steal all season. Here it is:
Yep, it was Crow-Armstrong, and it came when the situation demanded it—putting him at third with less than two outs, when he carried the tying run in the final inning of the game. In that contest, the Cubs stranded him there and lost; they let Crow-Armstrong down a lot this year. But he hadn't been afraid then, and he wouldn't be afraid this time, either.
This time, things broke just right for Chicago. Crow-Armstrong had the base stolen, anyway, but then the ball trickled away. It didn't even go that far; this was no airmailed ball into the left-field corner. It was enough, though. As soon as it began to roll away, Crow-Armstrong was off toward the plate. He had willed his team to a fourth straight win. It looked like the Summer of PCA might never end.
Baseball doesn't always reward such courage, even when paired with great talent. But the game is at its best when someone has the temerity and the instincts to get a delicate thing like that right. In fact, life is at its best in moments like that, when someone takes a bold chance in the service of both themselves and others and it pays off. The magic of Crow-Armstrong, this year, was distilled as gorgeously in that moment as in any other play he made—in the field, at bat, or on the bases. It felt a whole lot like when Báez scintillated with the same clutchness and fire and unstoppable talent, eight years ago.
I hadn't even initially thought of this, but now that I have, I feel compelled to include it. There was another moment akin to this one, in a way, from earlier in my baseball season—way earlier, back on May 20. It wasn't Crow-Armstrong making this particular play, but I had a better seat for it.
I know I don't want my children's personalities to be as closely wired to sports as mine was when I was their age. I don't know whether I want them to view Crow-Armstrong (whom I have found thoughtful, sharp and generous in my few interactions with him, and whom most people say means well even off the field) as a role model, except in the limited context of the game. However, what Crow-Armstrong has tapped into over the last three seasons in Chicago is the same vein of positive intensity that Báez brought years ago, and the legacy of that kind of intensity—of that level of care put into one's work, with a fierce joy held right at the surface and a focus on how what you're doing serves those around you—is a profoundly positive one. It runs deeper than wins and losses, and it extends even beyond a bitter playoff disappointment. The Summer of PCA will, in some ways, never end, even if there aren't great music videos out there of his highlight-reel plays. Sports fans are edified by consuming this kind of baseball. The benefits might even spill beyond the foul lines.

item.content:encoded:
After sweeping the Chicago Cubs in the NL Wild Card Series, the San Diego Padres have officially punched their ticket to the NLDS, where a matchup with the top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers awaits them. It will be the Brewers and Padres' first-ever meeting in the postseason, and there are no two hotter teams in baseball right now. The Brewers and Padres each posted a 18-6 record during the regular season portion of their September schedule, and San Diego added two more convincing wins over the Cubs this week.
While Brewers fans are relieved not to have to deal with the added stress that comes with facing the Cubs in the postseason, the Padres' recent performance undoubtedly has some fans wishing for a matchup with Craig Counsell's squad. That said, for as well as the Padres are playing right now, there are still certainly reasons for Brewers fans to be encouraged by the specific matchup. Let's take a closer look at three of the Padres' weaknesses and how they might come into play in the NLDS.
3 reasons Brewers fans should be encouraged by their NLDS matchup with the Padres
1. Question marks remain in San Diego's starting rotation
Heading into the postseason, the Padres' rotation was certainly their biggest weakness. With an elite bullpen and a surging offense, fans were unsure what San Diego would get from their starting staff in October. However, the duo of Michael King and Nick Pivetta, the latter of whom had a limited regular season workload this year due to an early-season elbow injury, dominated the Cubs in the Wild Card series, allowing just one earned run in a combined 10.1 innings. King's seven-inning shutout on Tuesday night did the heavy lifting, but Pivetta certainly impressed on Wednesday night as well.
However, even if King and Pivetta replicate their Wild Card performances in the NLDS -- likely in Games 2 and 3 -- questions remain in regard to the rest of San Diego's starting options. Trade deadline acquisitions Casey Mize, who is currently hurt, and Robbie Ray, who snuck onto the Wild Card roster but didn't pitch, haven't panned out as the Padres hoped they would. Long-time Los Angeles Dodger Walker Buehler also made the Padres' initial playoff roster, and is certainly a candidate to start a game, but his pedestrian 4.63 ERA in 32 starts this year doesn't necessarily scream "postseason starter." Not only will San Diego need King and Pivetta to repeat their incredible Wild Card performances in the NLDS, but they will also need another less obvious postseason starter to step up.
2. Padres' league-average infield defense bodes well for Brewers' offensive approach
The Cubs had an elite defensive unit in 2026, that much was obvious. In addition to Pete Crow-Armstrong's impressive performance in center field, the Cubs' infield of Alex Bregman (who was limited to DH in the Wild Card series due to a freak injury), Dansby Swanson, Nico Hoerner, and Michael Busch took away a number of would-be base hits thanks to their impressive range and sure-handedness. The Padres, while their infield unit is fine, by no means have the same elite ability to take away ground-ball base hits, and is therefore a better matchup for the Brewers' offense.
Manny Machado remains a strong defender when it comes to Outs Above Average (OAA), but his Defensive Runs Saved (DRS) total tells a different story. Ty France is a solid defensive first baseman, but the duo of Xander Bogaerts and Jake Cronenworth up the middle is below-average in the field. It's an important part of this series because the Brewers rank first in MLB in Batting Average on Balls in Play (BABIP), third in infield hits, and second in bunt hits. In other words, Milwaukee puts a lot of pressure on opposing infield defenses, and the Padres' shaky unit could come back to hurt them in this series.
3. San Diego's offense was far closer to league average for a majority of the season
The Padres' offense is on fire right now. No team posted a higher collective batting average, slugging percentage, or wRC+ than the Padres during the month of September, and only the Brewers scored more runs. Strong final months from Fernando Tatis Jr., Jackson Merrill, France, and Bogaerts led the Padres to these impressive numbers during the month of September, but for a majority of the season, San Diego's offense looked far closer to league average.
From the start of the season to the end of August, San Diego held a collective wRC+ of 98, indicating that their offensive unit was below league average for the first five months of the season. During that stretch, they ranked 20th in home runs and 22nd in runs scored. Their strong final push made their season-long numbers appear far better, but for a majority of the 2026 season, San Diego's offense was not among the best in baseball. That could matter not if the Padres' recent hot streak continues throughout October, but it's important to note this recent performance is the exception, not the norm.
2 reasons Brewers fans should be nervous about their NLDS matchup with the Padres
1. The Padres are the hottest team in baseball (aside from maybe the Brewers)
Whether their recent performance is the exception or not, there's no denying that the Padres are one of the two hottest teams in baseball, with their only threat being the team they will match up against in the NLDS. As previously mentioned, the Brewers and Padres finished first and second, respectively, in runs scored during the final month of the regular season en route to MLB-best 18-6 records. The Padres then stymied a strong Cubs' team with two comfortable wins in the NL Wild Card Series.
For the Brewers, who seemingly run into the hottest team in baseball in the early rounds of the postseason every single year, a matchup with the Padres feels like more bad luck. San Diego surged to the top Wild Card spot in the NL, secured a home postseason series, swept said series, and now carries that momentum into the NLDS. That certainly doesn't feel like a fair draw for the best team in baseball, who just completed a record-breaking 103-win regular season. Yes, the Padres have more flaws on their roster than the Brewers, but sometimes all that matters is how a team is playing when the postseason rolls around, to which the recent performance of each of these two teams would suggest fans are in for a competitive series.
2. San Diego is the only team with a better bullpen than the Brewers
The Brewers are heading into the postseason with their bullpen at its best, which is not often the case following the 162-game season. The combination of Trevor Megill, Abner Uribe, and Aaron Ashby at the back end, trade deadline acquisitions JoJo Romero and Antonio Senzatela in the middle innings, and multi-inning options like DL Hall, Chad Patrick, and Shane Drohan has Milwaukee's relief corps among the best in baseball as the playoffs arrive.
However, if there's one bullpen group that is better than the Brewers', it's the Padres' ridiculous assembly of relief weapons. Flame-throwing closer Mason Miller and his elite set-up man Adrian Morejon rightfully garner much of the attention, but other arms like Bradgley Rodriguez, Jason Adam, who just returned from the 60-day IL, and southpaw Yuki Matsui deserve respect as well. Given the strength of San Diego's bullpen and the question marks in their rotation, the pressure will be on the Brewers to build early leads and take advantage of as many scoring opportunities as possible.

item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO -- The lights cut out, Korn’s “Blind” blared, the sellout Petco Park crowd rose to their feet roaring and Mason Miller seemingly spawned onto the mound for the start of the ninth inning. The game was over. The National League Wild Card Series was over.
But in reality, it had ended well before that.
This is exactly why Padres general manager A.J. Preller assembled the best and deepest bullpen in baseball, for nights like Wednesday.
“In the postseason, you’ve got to get a lot of great hitters out,” Preller said. “You’ve got to have a lot of answers in that bullpen.”
After starter Nick Pivetta departed in the fourth, Padres manager Craig Stammen fully unleashed his bullpen over the final 5 2/3 innings against the Cubs in Game 2. Bradgley Rodriguez, Jason Adam, Adrian Morejon and Miller proceeded to allow just three men to reach base and keep Chicago’s league-best offense scoreless to slam the door on a 4-1 victory and send the Padres to the NL Division Series for a best-of-five-series against the Brewers.
Michael King going seven scoreless innings in Game 1 and saving the key arms in the back end set the Padres up perfectly to lean on that group the following night. If the Padres got an early lead, Stammen wasn’t going to mess around with keeping Pivetta in longer than he needed to secure the series.
That’s exactly how things played out.
San Diego scored a pair of runs in the second before Pivetta -- who did his job in limiting the Cubs over 3 1/3 innings -- got the hook in the fourth after giving up an RBI single to Nico Hoerner. A one-run lead ballooned to three after Gavin Sheets’ pinch-hit homer in the bottom half of the inning. The ‘pen took care of the rest.
“Michael’s effort last night was phenomenal and that allows us to go out firing in the early part of the game today and get our best guys out there,” Miller said. “It puts us in a really confident position. We get a lead and we feel really good about it.”
Perhaps the most important aspect of the Padres’ performance in this series was shutting down the Cubs’ elite lineup, and specifically their top two hitters in Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman. The former is coming off the seventh 40-40 season in baseball history and the latter posted a 1.010 OPS in the second half.
They collectively went 0-for-15 in the series with eight strikeouts.
It was quite the statement, but it’s exactly what the Padres have been doing all season. By innings, San Diego had the fourth-most used bullpen in the Majors (683 2/3) and it possessed the fifth-best ERA (3.53).
“It’s an incredible group, top to bottom,” Adam said. “It doesn’t matter the situation, it doesn’t matter the inning, everybody out there is ready to go at all times. Fourth inning, ninth inning, I don’t care who we put out there, I feel really confident the guy is getting the job done.”
Rodriguez was the first into the fray, the rookie right-hander who immediately became one of the best relief arms in the sport and has been dominant in high-leverage situations throughout the year. He played fireman in the fourth, escaping a bases-loaded jam to preserve Pivetta’s line before pitching a clean fifth that he capped with a strikeout of Seiya Suzuki on a changeup below the zone.
“We’ve always known that about Bradgley -- that his maturity level is beyond his years,” Padres pitching coach Ruben Niebla said. “He doesn’t rattle. He doesn’t get nervous. He trusts himself and is a confident guy. We’re able to put him in those situations very confidently, and he’s responded well to that.”
Adam got through a 1-2-3 sixth, then Morejon cruised through the seventh and eighth, allowing just one hit, a Tyrone Taylor single. Then the ball was handed to Miller, the most imposing reliever in the game, who struck out an insane 47.4% of the batters he faced this season and finished with a career-best 1.67 ERA and 38 saves.
He gave up a double to Hoerner but struck out a pair and got Carson Kelly to ground out to end it, sending the Padres to Milwaukee and the Cubs back home.
“It’s not about any individual, it’s about a group,” Miller said. “It’s about passing the ball to the next guy and getting us in the clubhouse with a win. I think it’s a lot of selfless guys down there.”
Now, the Padres get the top-seeded Brewers in the NLDS, another team with plenty of firepower in the bullpen. To defeat them, and anyone else standing in the Padres’ way this October, Wednesday will be the template.
And if it continues to pan out the way it did, that should scare the rest of the postseason field.
“We knew we had six innings we could cover,” Niebla said. “It worked out to perfection.”

item.content:encoded:
What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa.
The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the postseason on Wednesday so let’s jump straight into the action!
AL Wild Card Series Game 2
Chicago White Sox 7, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago wins 2-0)
After just two games, I can’t think of any playoff participant who wants to face these White Sox. That is a sentence that no one could conceive of typing at the start of the season. Two seasons removed from suffering the most losses in MLB history and on the back of three straight losing campaigns, this upstart Chicago squad came out of nowhere to crash the postseason, starting with a two game sweep of the Astros in their own building.
They have done so by scoring early and often, the White Sox lineup a deep unit one-thru-nine with multiple ways to hurt you. They work deep counts, foul pitches off, draw walks, and can put the ball in play, but can also slug the ball out of the yard from almost any spot in the batting order. On Tuesday, they scored three unanswered runs in the first two innings to put the Astros on the back foot from the word go, and Wednesday continued the trend with the Southsiders hanging a four-spot before the home team had a chance to bat.
They had a 1-0 lead just five pitches into the game against Astros ace Hunter Brown, Sam Antonacci leading off with a double before Kyle Teel drove him home with a single. A fielding error by Nick Allen on a Miguel Vargas grounder put a pair on, and three straight singles by Andrew Benintendi, Tristan Peters, and Chase Meidroth plated three more runs with help from a Lucas Spence throwing error from center.
Credit to the Astros, they did not roll over after going down four in the first and slowly chipped into the White Sox lead. Jeremy Peña led off the bottom of the first with a booming home run that clattered off the left field wall just below the train tracks. Cam Smith hit one to almost exactly the same spot with two outs in the second. Jose Altuve narrowly snuck a solo shot into the Crawford Boxes to lead off the fourth and just like that, a 4-0 game had become a 4-3 thriller.
An inning later it looked like the Astros would pull of the improbable and complete the comeback. Smith was hit by a pitch, Peña singled, and Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases with two outs for Altuve. However, reliever Anthony Kay got Altuve to fly out to medium right field to strand all three ducks on the pond. That left the door open for the White Sox to swing the momentum back in their own favor and they did so immediately. Benintendi and Peters drew a pair of walks to open the sixth, prompting Joe Espada to call on Bryan Abreu out of the bullpen. Astros owner Jim Crane vetoed a trade of Abreu to the Twins in the final minutes of the deadline, and Abreu rewarded that faith by hanging a 3-1 slider to Meidroth, the second baseman crushing a three-run bomb to left to put the final nail in the Astros’ coffin.
After sweeping this rematch of the 2005 World Series, the White Sox advance to the ALDS where they will face the AL Central champion Guardians, first pitch of Game 1 scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET on Saturday.
NL Wild Card Series Game 2
Philadelphia Phillies 4, Atlanta Braves 3
(Series tied 1-1)
The Phillies’ season was hanging by a thread until some late heroics by Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Alec Bohm sent this thrilling series to a decisive Game 3. It was a pitchers’ duel early between two starters trending in opposite directions. Tyler Mahle entered his first career playoff start with a sub-two ERA after joining the Braves from the Giants at the deadline while Cristopher Sánchez posted an ERA above five in the month of September (though will still likely wrap up his second straight runner-up finish in NL Cy Young balloting).
The one thing the two starters do have in common is first inning struggles and that certainly played out in this game. Mahle allowed a leadoff double to Trea Turner and consecutive one-out singles by Bryce Harper and Alex Bohm to allow the Phillies to jump ahead, 1-0. However, Sánchez issued a leadoff walk to Ronald Acuña Jr., who promptly stole second and scored the tying run on a Matt Olson single.
Both starters settled in from there, trading zeroes for the next five innings, until things unraveled for Sánchez and his defense in the seventh. Sean Murphy worked a leadoff walk and Ha-Seong Kim reached on a bunt single to put a pair on with no outs. Drake Baldwin then clubbed what looked like a routine liner to right, but Harper misplayed it horrifically breaking in on the ball only to watch it sail over his glove and to the wall for what was ruled as an RBI double. Sánchez intentionally walked Ozzie Albies to load the bases, and Olson made him pay with a sac fly to double the Braves lead, 3-1.
What should have been a hammer blow to the Phillies morale did not play out as such. Schwarber immediately responded with a towering leadoff shot off lefty reliever Dylan Lee, and Harper atoned for his misplay by going back-to-back to retie the game, 3-3. That sent this game to extra innings, where the much-maligned Alec Bohm continued his redemption tour. Bohm was on the bubble of being non-tendered during the offseason, but the Phillies kept him around and drove in the first run of the series with an RBI double in the first inning of Game 1. The third baseman was the ultimate hero in this one, his opposite field solo homer off rookie Didier Fuentes in the 10th to keep the Phillies season alive and force a decisive Game 3.
San Diego Padres 4, Chicago Cubs 1
(San Diego wins 2-0)
This game featured surprisingly quick hooks of both starters as neither manager wanted to risk leaving their highest leverage relievers unused. One was certainly more deserved than the other, Kevin Gausman allowing three runs on five hits in 3.1 innings. The Cubs were desperate for starting pitching at the Trade Deadline and Gausman was supposed to be their big prize. However, he flopped after making the move from the Blue Jays, pitching to a 4.83 ERA in nine starts post-deadline, and his stinker tonight was the beginning of the end of the Cubs’ season. Nick Pivetta on the other hand held Chicago to a run on three hits and two walks with four strikeouts in 3.1 innings, but Craig Stammen seemed determined to play the matchups in this one.
Ty France got things started with a double to lead off the second, advancing to third on a Jackson Merrill single, who then stole second to put a pair in scoring position for Xander Bogaerts. The veteran shortstop opened the scoring with an RBI single, which brought Ethan Salas to the plate. The 20-year-old became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a playoff game, and in his first postseason PA, he lifted a sac fly to center to plate Merrill as the Padres’ second run.
The real story of this series has been the Cubs’ inability to score. They led MLB scoring 5.25 runs per game, spearheaded by shoo-in NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and his MLB-leading 45 home runs (PCA would go 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series). They found themselves shut out through the first 12.1 innings of this series, finally breaking the seal in the fourth on a Seiya Suzuki single, Ian Happ walk, and Nico Hoerner RBI single. A Carson Kelly hit-by-pitch loaded the bases with two outs, but Dansby Swanson flew out to stand all three in place.
San Diego immediately punished them for failing to fully cash in on that scoring opportunity. Bogaerts reached on a one-out double, prompting Craig Counsell to call on Daniel Palencia in relief of Gausman. Palencia yanked a 101 mph fastball right into Sheets’ nitro zone down and in, and the lefty crushed it to right for a mammoth two-run blast.
It was all hands on deck from there from the Padres bullpen looking to protect their lead for the final five innings of the contest. They proved how terrifying a relief corps they’ve been all season, allowing just three base runners — a Michael Busch walk with two outs in the fifth, a Tyrone Taylor pinch-hit single with one out in the eighth, and a Hoerner one-out double off Mason Miller in the ninth — after the Cubs stranded the bases loaded to end the fourth.
San Diego advances to the NLDS where they will face the best team in baseball. It’s an unenviable position to come up against presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski and the 103-win Brewers. Game 1 of that series is scheduled for October 3rd with first pitch time contingent upon the result of Game 3 between Philly and Atlanta.

item.content:encoded:
After a disappointing 93-loss season, Royals president of baseball operations J.J. Picollo said the team plans to be “aggressive in acquisitions.” But that aggressiveness, he cautioned, should not be confused with a willingness to spend aggressively on the payroll. He addressed the media along with manager Matt Quatraro in the team’s annual end-of-year press conference on Wednesday.
The season did not go as planned, with the team stumbling to a 12-19 start by the end of April. Picollo took addressed the slow start by saying “we’re responsible for the performance in April and May.” He did point out the World Baseball Classic kept some Royals players away from the team during spring training, making it more difficult to build team camaraderie. And injuries made it difficult for the team to climb their way out of the hole they had dug.
“We weren’t very good in April, and we weren’t very good in the beginning of May. I can’t sit here and tell you that I know we would have been good in June, July, August, and September, but if we had had those players on our roster and healthy and available, I think we could have made a better run.”
The Royals lost key players like Maikel Garcia and Vinnie Pasquantino early in the year, in addition to having their pitching staff decimated by injuries over the summer. The Royals announced changes to their medical staff, although Picollo denied the injuries were the reason for the moves. He also contended that despite all the adversity, the team has to win.
“That being said, nobody feels sorry for you. You got to go out and win.”
Here is what Picollo had to say about how he plans to address team needs this offseason.
The bullpen
”The bullpen is going to be a focus for us,” said Picollo. “There’s no question.”
Royals relievers had a 5.07 ERA, second-worst in baseball, and a league-worst 6.65 ERA in the ninth inning. The team lost closer Carlos Estévez to injury after his first game, and got disappointing performances from Lucas Erceg and Matt Strahm.
While Picollo expects the team to be aggressive, he added “I don’t want that mistaken for aggressive payroll spending.” He noted that the team was top five in spending on the bullpen over the last three years, but that spending on relievers may not be the solution due to the volatility of their performance.
“We have to look into ways at being more efficient,” he said, adding that they tried to look for that “diamond in the rough” late this year with waiver claims and small deals. They sought pitchers that presented different arm angles and pitches to give hitters varying looks.
“There’s not a clear, definitive answer on how to pull put a bullpen together. But I think the variety of ‘different looks,’ ‘different stuff’ type of relievers is the way we’re probably going to go.”
Back in August, owner John Sherman said he thought the bullpen could be “cobbled” together without spending too much money.
While Picollo highlighted the pitching of Steven Cruz and Nate Pearson down the stretch, the 2027 closer may not be on the roster right now.
“I don’t know if we’ll be able to sit here today and tell you we’ll have a closer. Internally, we don’t think we necessarily have it.”
Daniel Lynch IV, who enjoyed a breakthrough season in the bullpen, will be given a chance to compete for a starting spot next year. Lynch had a 1.96 ERA in 46 relief appearances this year, and a 6.53 ERA in 10 starts.
Starting pitching
Picollo said starting depth was their biggest priority after upgrading the bullpen. He admitted that the starting pitching depth he had amassed before the season was not nearly enough.
“It was as confident as I’ve ever been in starting pitching depth,” he said before discussing the injuries that hit the pitching staff. Cole Ragans, Kris Bubic, Ryan Bergert, and Stephen Kolek all missed significant time this season.
“So we’re never going to take starting pitching for granted.”
Next year’s rotation will feature Michael Wacha, Seth Lugo, and Noah Cameron, but the team will have to figure out who will fill the last two spots. The team expects to pick up the option of Tony Gonsolin, the former Dodgers All-Star pitcher who was signed late in the year and pitched in one game for the Royals. He could compete for a rotation spot along with Lynch, and Randy Dobnak, who impressed with a 3.51 ERA in 15 games.
Offense
As far as the offense, Picollo liked some of the underlying things they did, but ultimately the team did not score enough runs, particularly on the road. The Royals averaged 4.26 runs per game overall, finishing 21st in baseball. That was a slight improvement over their performance in 2025 when they scored 4.02 runs per game, 26th in baseball. But they finished dead last in baseball in runs on the road, averaging just 3.62 per game.
“It’s a combination of things. It’s getting on base at a greater clip. It’s running the bases well. It’s putting the ball in play when you need to with a man in scoring position. A lot is made of batting average with runners in scoring position - for us its more about ‘did you get him in?’”
He confirmed Ken Rosenthal’s report from Tuesday that hitting coach Alec Zumwalt has been reassigned to focus more on minor league development, but Picollo clarified that this was not a reflection of performance, and had been the plan all along. Zumwalt had worked with the current core of Royals hitters in the minors, and had ascended to the big league level with them. The team wants him back working with young minor league hitters, while assistant hitting coaches Marcus Thames and Connor Dawson work with the big league hitters. The Royals will likely hire another assistant hitting coach, but Picollo backed the work of Zumwalt.
“We’re not disappointed with his performance. We think he’s a very good hitting coach.”
The team will look for offensive upgrades in the outfield. Picollo noted the outfield defense regressed this season, despite the fences at Kauffman Stadium being moved in leaving less room to cover. Outfield prospect Carson Roccaforte could be in the mix, although he is left-handed and Picollo noted that the team is already very left-handed heavy.
The team will be “open to any and all ideas” on trades, even if that means trading players on the roster. Picollo added he is not interested in trading players for prospects, given their timeline and expectations to contend.
“We need to add players that help us at the major league level.”
Spending
Picollo said he does not have a specific payroll figure, but noted that ownership has approved additional spending when he has brought forward opportunities worth pursuing.
“I’ve always felt like it’s not my job to worry about the payroll. Our job is to get the most out of whatever we have,” said Picollo, noting there are teams in the playoffs with lower payrolls than the Royals, while many teams that spent a lot are sitting at home.
“I don’t think payroll is indicative of success on the field. I think success on the field comes with knowing your roster and how to get the most out of your roster and that’s our task. That’s what we need to do.”
Sherman said in August that the team is “freeing up some money” the team could invest, with about $30 million expected to come off the payroll with impending free agents.
When asked about potential long-term contracts for Jac Caglianone or Carter Jensen, Picollo deferred, saying that they typically don’t seriously consider such deals until after a player’s second year of service time. Both players just completed their first full season in the big leagues, finishing strong with each hitting over 20 home runs and posting an OPS+ over 120.
The Royals may have to work quickly to address their shortcomings simply because of the looming potential work stoppage. The collective bargaining agreement expires on December 1, which could lead to an end to free agent signings until a new labor deal is worked out.
“The aggressiveness in November is going to be important for us, as we expect the entire industry to be fairly busy.”
But it is clear the Royals have a lot do before the next season begins. The Royals entered 2026 expecting to build on back-to-back winning seasons. Instead, they finished with the fifth-worst record in baseball and now face significant questions in the bullpen, starting rotation and outfield. Picollo acknowledged that the fans demand more.
“It’s refreshing to know that our fans have high expectations. We want them to have high expectations, because we gave them reason to have high expectations,” said Picollo.
“With that comes to responsibility of getting it done. I think we feel pressure every year to win.”

item.content:encoded:
In a series that is shaping up to be another instant classic between the bitter NL East rivals, it now all comes down to Game 3 on Thursday. A Phillies win would set up an NLDS rematch from last year against the Dodgers, while the Braves hope to punch their ticket to the NLDS for the first time since 2023.
“Just win a game,” said Phillies infielder Alec Bohm, who hit the game-winning homer in the Phillies’ 4-3 extra-inning victory in Game 2. “ … I think as much as we want to enjoy this for a little bit, it's the same as we did [after Game 1]: Turn the page, and move on to tomorrow and show up ready to do the same thing.”
So, what could the Phillies and Braves possibly have in store for their winner-take-all showdown?
While that’s the biggest question looming over the National League Wild Card Series, it’s far from the only one. Here’s everything you need to know about Game 3:
When is the game and how can I watch it?
The game will begin at 8 p.m. ET and air on NBC and Peacock.
The Wild Card Series will be available in Spanish on Universo, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games, beginning with the Wild Card Series.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Phillies: TBD
The Phillies planned to meet following Game 2 to discuss their pitching plans for this week’s third elimination game. Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said Monday that Aaron Nola was setting up to start Game 3, but there’s no question things can change. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see ace Zack Wheeler start on short rest. If he doesn’t start, there’s no doubt he’d enter the game in relief.
Braves: TBD
Grant Holmes will attempt to handle the bulk of the innings. But the Braves haven’t said whether he’ll start or possibly follow an opener. The top options to open are left-handers Ray Kerr or Brent Suter. Either would be tasked with handling Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber in the first inning.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Braves: The Braves’ lineup appears much more formidable against right-handed pitchers. With Mike Yastrzemski in left field, Mauricio Dubón would move to shortstop, which was where Ha-Seong Kim started during the first two games.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Phillies: Mattingly said it’s “all hands on deck,” although closer Jhoan Duran wasn’t available in Game 2. Mattingly said he hoped he’d have Duran in Game 3. But other than Cristopher Sánchez, who started Game 2, probably every pitcher on the Phillies’ staff will be available in some capacity in Game 3. That’s everybody from Wheeler to Luzardo to Painter.
Braves: Closer Raisel Iglesias and his top setup men Didier Fuentes and Dylan Lee both pitched in the first two games of this series. Each should be available in this winner-take-all game. Robert Suarez hasn’t been utilized yet. He missed three months with an elbow ailment before making two appearances last week. But manager Walt Weiss may have no other choice but to turn to the right-hander, who posted a 0.56 ERA in 31 appearances before his elbow became a problem in June.
Any injuries of note?
Braves: OF Lane Thomas could be available during the NLDS. Starting pitchers Bryce Elder (arthroscopic knee surgery), Reynaldo López (right shoulder inflammation) and Martín Pérez (lower back discomfort) may also be available in future rounds.
Who is hot and who is not?
Phillies: Home runs often come in bunches for Schwarber and Harper. Did their back-to-back homers in the eighth inning in Game 2 get them going? Bohm is 3-for-8 with one double and one home run in the series. After struggling all season, Realmuto has two hits and two RBIs this series.
Anything else fans might want to know?
The Phillies are 1-3 in franchise history in win-or-go-home postseason games. They won Game 5 of the 1980 NLCS. They lost Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS, Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS and Game 5 of the 1981 NLDS.

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Six outs away from finally killing Philadelphia’s hex, the Braves were undone by their bullpen, the portion of their roster that was supposed to be a postseason strength.
“I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers of all time,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. Every once in a while, they get you.”
Nearly 40 years later, Weiss still remembers the sting he and his A’s teammates felt when an injured Gibson came off the bench to hit a walk-off homer against Hall of Fame closer Dennis Eckersley in Game 1 of the 1988 World Series at Dodger Stadium.
A similar type of sting was felt as the Braves blew a two-run eighth-inning lead in a 4-3, 10-inning loss to the Phillies in Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series on Wednesday afternoon at Truist Park. Dylan Lee surrendered consecutive homers to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper in the eighth. Didier Fuentes allowed Alec Bohm’s decisive homer with two outs in the 10th.
“That's life,” Braves starting pitcher Tyler Mahle said. “Sometimes, it happens. There's nothing really else to say about it. It sucks now, but we're going to have a chance to go out there tomorrow and turn it around.”
Now, Weiss’ bunch must win Game 3 on Thursday to avoid being eliminated from the playoffs by Philadelphia for the fourth time overall and third time in the past five years. The Phillies eliminated Atlanta teams that won 100-plus regular-season games in 1993 (NLCS), 2022 (NLDS) and 2023 (NLDS).
Thursday's Game 3, airing on NBC and Peacock, will start at 8 p.m. ET.
“[The Braves] have played great at home,” Harper said. “But again, I'll just talk about the postseason; it's just a different animal.”
Mahle proved he was up to the challenge during what was his first postseason appearance. The right-hander, acquired from the Giants on Aug. 2, became the first Braves pitcher to allow one run or none over seven-plus innings in the postseason since Max Fried threw seven scoreless against the Reds in Game 1 of the 2020 NL Wild Card Series.
Once Harper misplayed a Drake Baldwin fly ball into a go-ahead double off Phillies starter Cristopher Sánchez during Atlanta’s two-run seventh, it looked like the Braves were destined for a great storyline.
But instead of celebrating how their trade acquisition helped them end the Phillies’ playoff dominance, the Braves were reminded that Lee hasn’t been nearly as good as he was before the All-Star break, when he posted a 1.47 ERA in 43 innings (44 appearances).
When Schwarber opened the eighth with a Statcast-projected 447-foot homer and Harper followed by depositing another ball into the right-field seats, Lee extended the troubles he had while posting a 6.00 ERA in 24 innings after the break. It should be noted he allowed just two homers during that stretch, and he did not allow any home runs to left-handed batters during the regular season.
“Lee’s our high-leverage lefty,” Weiss said. “He put down the same part of the order yesterday.”
Lee struck out Schwarber and got Harper to fly out in Game 1. How might he fare if he’s asked to go through these left-handed sluggers for a third straight day?
How about Fuentes? The rookie right-hander was masterful during the regular season, posting a 2.05 ERA in 70 1/3 innings as a reliever. But he surrendered J.T. Realmuto’s two-run triple in Game 1, and his psyche was bruised again Wednesday when Bohm sneaked his game-winning homer over the right-field wall.
“[Fuentes] made a good pitch,” Baldwin said. “I think if we need him tomorrow, he'll be ready to go, and I don't think he'll let that affect him too much.”
The Phillies’ rotation was a concern entering this series because Zack Wheeler was needed to pitch on Sunday with a postseason spot on the line. Well, Aaron Nola and Wheeler could be used in Game 3.
As for the Braves, they haven’t announced who will start Game 3. Grant Holmes will be lined up to pitch at least four innings. But will he start? Or will either Ray Kerr or Brent Suter take the mound as an opener?
More importantly, can the Braves bounce back from this and finally end their playoff struggles against their division rivals?
